explanations.explanation: That's the job, friend. Mark quotes Isaiah the prophet: "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way." Think of it like a baker who sets out the bowls and heats the oven before the dough ever shows up. The messenger's work happens before the main event.
I can see why a messenger sounds like a guard, but that's not what the text says. The words say this messenger goes ahead to "…prepare Your way." Guarding gates isn't anywhere in the verse.

Counting sounds official, so I get the guess. But Mark 1:2 never mentions a head count. The messenger is sent ahead of Him "…who will prepare Your way." That's about getting things ready for the One coming.

Right on the money, baker. The voice is calling in the wilderness, "Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him." Those straight paths are right there in Mark 1:3. Mark is telling us the Lord is coming, and the way needs to be ready.

This one is true, friend. The voice in the wilderness says, "Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him." Those straight paths are right there in verse 3. It's an easy one to doubt when it sounds so simple.

explanations.answer: A baptism for the forgiveness of sins
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Mark says John was "…preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." Repentance means turning from sin, and John's baptism went with that. That's the message he's shouting out in the wilderness.

explanations.answer: A new temple for the people to build
explanations.explanation: A building project would keep a crowd busy, I'll give you that. But John isn't talking about construction at all. Mark 1:4 says he preaches "…a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." His message is about people's sins being forgiven.

explanations.answer: A tax to rebuild the city walls
explanations.explanation: A tax would make for a short sermon, friend, with a long line of people leaving. Mark 1:4 says John is "…preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins." No tax and no walls are in that verse. Forgiveness is the message.

I see why you picked it, but it's the other way around. Mark 1:5 says, "Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River." So the people did confess, and the baptism came with it. This statement is false.

Yes, baker! Mark 1:5 says, "Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River." They confessed their sins, and they were baptized. So the statement that they don't confess is false.
That's the menu, friend. Mark 1:6 says, "His food was locusts and wild honey." Locusts are insects, and the honey is wild. I've burned some batches in my day, but even my worst one beats that.
Bread and fish is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't what the text says. Mark 1:6 says, "His food was locusts and wild honey." It's a wilderness menu, through and through.
Lamb and bitter herbs is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't on John's menu. Mark 1:6 says, "His food was locusts and wild honey." That's what he eats out in the wilderness.

explanations.answer: Not worthy to untie His sandals
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. John says, "…the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie." That's John, a man the whole countryside came out to see, saying he isn't even worthy for that small job. He knows who's coming after him.

explanations.answer: Chosen to carry His royal crown
explanations.explanation: A crown carrier sounds like an honor, but John doesn't say anything like that. He says the straps of this One's sandals are something he is "…not worthy to stoop down and untie." He lowers himself, not raises himself.

explanations.answer: Sent to stand at His right hand
explanations.explanation: The right hand is a big spot, and John doesn't claim it. In Mark 1:7 he says he isn't "…worthy to stoop down and untie." the straps of the sandals. That's about as low as a position gets, and he says it about himself.
Water it is, friend. John says in Mark 1:8, "I baptize you with water…" And he does it in the Jordan River, as verse 5 says. Then he points ahead to One who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.
Oil is a good guess, since it's a thing people use in the Bible. But that's not what John says here. In Mark 1:8 he says, "I baptize you with water…" The Jordan River is right there in the story.
Ashes feel serious, and this is a serious moment, so I see the pull. But John says, "I baptize you with water…" People are going down into the Jordan River, and water is what they find there.
I can see why you'd think that, since John says One greater than himself is coming. But Mark 1:9 says Jesus "…was baptized by John in the Jordan." John doesn't send Him away. This one is false.
That's right, baker. Mark 1:9 says Jesus "…was baptized by John in the Jordan." He came from Nazareth in Galilee and went into the water. John doesn't turn Him away.
Yes, friend. Mark 1:10 says Jesus "…saw the heavens breaking open and the Spirit descending on Him like a dove." The Spirit is what comes down, and it comes "…like a dove." It's a gentle picture.
A pillar of fire shows up in Exodus 13:21, but not in this scene. In Mark 1:10, Jesus sees "…the Spirit descending on Him like a dove." It's a quiet image, nothing blazing.
A bright cloud would be a big entrance, and I get why it came to mind. But Mark 1:10 says what Jesus sees is "…the Spirit descending on Him like a dove." That's the answer from the text.

That's right, baker. The voice from heaven says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased." Those words are for Jesus, and Mark records them (Mark 1:11). Beloved Son is exactly what the voice calls Him.
This one is true, friend. Mark 1:11 says a voice came from heaven: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased." The words "beloved Son" are right there. No need to second-guess this one.
Wilderness is it, friend. Mark 1:12 says, "At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness…" It happens right after the baptism. Verse 13 then tells us what happens out there.
The temple is a natural place to go next, I'll give you that. But Mark 1:12 says, "At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness…" He's out in the open land, not in a building.
A city would at least have a few people around, and I understand the guess. But Mark 1:12 says the Spirit drove Jesus "…into the wilderness…" That's where verse 13 puts Him with the wild animals.
Forty, baker! Mark 1:13 says, "…He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan." Forty days is a long stretch to be out there. And the verse says He wasn't there alone.
Seven is a fair guess, but it isn't the number here. Mark 1:13 says, "…He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan." The number in this verse is forty.
Three days is a number people know from other parts of the Bible, so I get it. But in this verse, Mark 1:13 says, "…He was there for forty days…" That's way more than three, friend.
That's the one, baker. Mark 1:13 says, "…the angels ministered to Him." To minister means to serve and care for. So even out there with the wild animals, the angels were with Jesus.
The testing in this verse is done by Satan, not the angels. Mark 1:13 says Jesus was "…being tempted by Satan." and then, "…the angels ministered to Him." The angels are on a different job, friend.
Staying back sounds careful, but that's not what the verse says. Mark 1:13 says, "…the angels ministered to Him." That means they served Him, which is a lot closer than keeping their distance.
